## Proof

Let $Q = \operatorname{pos}(x^1, x^6) = \{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2 : a\ge 0,\, b\ge 0\}$ be the closed first quadrant. The five cones $C_i=\operatorname{pos}(x^i,x^{i+1})$, $i=1,\dots,5$, partition $Q$: the rays $x^1,\dots,x^6$ appear in order of increasing slope ($0,1,2,3,4,\infty$), so consecutive cones share exactly one edge and their union is $Q$.

**Step 1 — The matrices are correct and unimodular.** A direct check gives $A^i x^i = y^i$ and $A^i x^{i+1}=y^{i+1}$ for $i=1,\dots,5$:

| $i$ | $A^i x^i$ | $=y^i$ | $A^i x^{i+1}$ | $=y^{i+1}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $(1,0)$ | $y^1$✓ | $(0,1)$ | $y^2$✓ |
| 2 | $(0,1)$ | $y^2$✓ | $(-1,0)$ | $y^3$✓ |
| 3 | $(-1,0)$ | $y^3$✓ | $(0,-1)$ | $y^4$✓ |
| 4 | $(0,-1)$ | $y^4$✓ | $(1,0)$ | $y^5$✓ |
| 5 | $(1,0)$ | $y^5$✓ | $(0,1)$ | $y^6$✓ |

The determinants are $\det A^1=1$, $\det A^2=(-1)+2=1$, $\det A^3=3-2=1$, $\det A^4=-3+4=1$, $\det A^5=1$. Hence every piece is invertible and orientation-preserving, so $f$ is coherently oriented.

**Step 2 — Image of $Q$ under $f$.** Since $A^i$ maps $C_i$ linearly onto $\operatorname{pos}(y^i,y^{i+1})$, the image of $C_i$ is the closed quadrant

$$\operatorname{pos}(y^i,y^{i+1}) =
\begin{cases}
Q_1=\{(a,b):a\ge0,b\ge0\}, & i=1,\\
Q_2=\{(a,b):a\le0,b\ge0\}, & i=2,\\
Q_3=\{(a,b):a\le0,b\le0\}, & i=3,\\
Q_4=\{(a,b):a\ge0,b\le0\}, & i=4,\\
Q_1, & i=5.
\end{cases}$$

Thus $f(Q)=Q_1\cup Q_2\cup Q_3\cup Q_4=\mathbb R^2$, with $Q_1$ covered **twice** (by $C_1$ and $C_5$) and $Q_2,Q_3,Q_4$ covered **once** each.

**Step 3 — Boundary consistency.** On the boundary of $Q$: $A^1(t,0)=(t,0)$ on the $x^1$-ray and $A^5(0,t)=(0,t)$ on the $x^6$-ray, so $f$ is the identity on $\partial Q$. This agrees with the identity definition on $\mathbb R^2\setminus Q$, so $f$ is well defined and continuous.

**Step 4 — Counting preimages of a nonzero $v$.** Because each $A^i$ is invertible, each cone $C_i$ contributes **at most one** preimage of $v$ (the unique solution of $A^i z=v$ lying in $C_i$). Outside $Q$, $f=\mathrm{id}$ contributes one preimage exactly when $v\notin Q$.

*Interior of $Q_1$:* $v$ lies in the images of $C_1$ and $C_5$ only. The two preimages lie in $C_1=\operatorname{pos}(x^1,x^2)$ and $C_5=\operatorname{pos}(x^5,x^6)$, which are disjoint sectors, so they are **distinct**. Since $v\in Q$, the identity region contributes $0$. **Total: $2$.**

*Interior of $Q_2$ (resp. $Q_3$, $Q_4$):* $v$ lies in exactly one cone image ($C_2$, $C_3$, $C_4$ resp.), giving $1$ preimage in $Q$. Also $v\notin Q$, so the identity contributes $1$ more (the point $v$ itself, which is distinct from the preimage in $Q$ since the latter lies in $Q$). **Total: $2$.**

*Positive $x$-axis, $v=(a,0)$, $a>0$:* In $Q_1$. From $C_1$: $A^1(a,0)=(a,0)$, preimage $(a,0)\in C_1$ (on edge $x^1$). From $C_5$: $A^5(a,4a)=(a,0)$, preimage $(a,4a)=a\,x^5\in C_5$ (on edge $x^5$). These are distinct; identity contributes $0$. **Total: $2$.**

*Positive $y$-axis, $v=(0,b)$, $b>0$:* From $C_1$: $A^1(b,b)=(0,b)$, preimage $(b,b)=b\,x^2\in C_1$. From $C_5$: $A^5(0,b)=(0,b)$, preimage $(0,b)\in C_5$ (on edge $x^6$). Distinct; identity $0$. **Total: $2$.**

*Negative $x$-axis, $v=(-a,0)$, $a>0$:* Lies in $\partial Q_2\cap\partial Q_3$. From $C_2$: $A^2(a,2a)=(-a,0)$, preimage $a\,x^3\in C_2$. From $C_3$: $A^3(a,2a)=(-a,0)$, preimage $a\,x^3\in C_3$ — the **same point** (the shared edge $x^3$, where $A^2$ and $A^3$ agree because both send $x^3\mapsto y^3$). So $1$ preimage in $Q$. Since $v\notin Q$, identity adds $v$ itself. **Total: $2$.**

*Negative $y$-axis, $v=(0,-b)$, $b>0$:* Similarly, $C_3$ and $C_4$ share edge $x^4$; $A^3(b,3b)=A^4(b,3b)=(0,-b)$, giving one preimage $b\,x^4$ in $Q$. Identity adds $v$. **Total: $2$.**

**Step 5 — The origin.** $f(0)=0$ from every piece, and $0\in Q$ so the identity region gives nothing extra: the origin has exactly **one** preimage (itself). This is why the statement excludes $v=0$.

**Conclusion.** Every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^2$ has exactly two preimages under $f$; in particular $f$ is two-to-one on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ and hence **not injective**, despite being coherently oriented (all pieces unimodular with $\det=+1$). This exhibits the failure of the converse of "injective PL map ⇒ coherently oriented" in dimension $2$. $\blacksquare$

The five cones $C_i=\operatorname{pos}(x^i,x^{i+1})$, $i=1,\dots,5$, partition $Q$: the rays $x^1,\dots,x^6$ appear in order of increasing slope ($0,1,2,3,4,\infty$), so consecutive cones share exactly one edge and their union is $Q$.

**Step 1 — The matrices are correct and unimodular.** A direct check gives $A^i x^i = y^i$ and $A^i x^{i+1}=y^{i+1}$ for $i=1,\dots,5$:

| $i$ | $A^i x^i$ | $=y^i$ | $A^i x^{i+1}$ | $=y^{i+1}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $(1,0)$ | $y^1$✓ | $(0,1)$ | $y^2$✓ |
| 2 | $(0,1)$ | $y^2$✓ | $(-1,0)$ | $y^3$✓ |
| 3 | $(-1,0)$ | $y^3$✓ | $(0,-1)$ | $y^4$✓ |
| 4 | $(0,-1)$ | $y^4$✓ | $(1,0)$ | $y^5$✓ |
| 5 | $(1,0)$ | $y^5$✓ | $(0,1)$ | $y^6$✓ |

The determinants are $\det A^1=1$, $\det A^2=(-1)+2=1$, $\det A^3=3-2=1$, $\det A^4=-3+4=1$, $\det A^5=1$. Hence every piece is invertible and orientation-preserving, so $f$ is coherently oriented.

**Step 2 — Image of $Q$ under $f$.** Since $A^i$ maps $C_i$ linearly onto $\operatorname{pos}(y^i,y^{i+1})$, the image of $C_i$ is the closed quadrant

$$\operatorname{pos}(y^i,y^{i+1}) =
\begin{cases}
Q_1=\{(a,b):a\ge0,b\ge0\}, & i=1,\\
Q_2=\{(a,b):a\le0,b\ge0\}, & i=2,\\
Q_3=\{(a,b):a\le0,b\le0\}, & i=3,\\
Q_4=\{(a,b):a\ge0,b\le0\}, & i=4,\\
Q_1, & i=5.
\end{cases}$$

Thus $f(Q)=Q_1\cup Q_2\cup Q_3\cup Q_4=\mathbb R^2$, with $Q_1$ covered **twice** (by $C_1$ and $C_5$) and $Q_2,Q_3,Q_4$ covered **once** each.

**Step 3 — Boundary consistency.** On the boundary of $Q$: $A^1(t,0)=(t,0)$ on the $x^1$-ray and $A^5(0,t)=(0,t)$ on the $x^6$-ray, so $f$ is the identity on $\partial Q$. This agrees with the identity definition on $\mathbb R^2\setminus Q$, so $f$ is well defined and continuous.

**Step 4 — Counting preimages of a nonzero $v$.** Because each $A^i$ is invertible, each cone $C_i$ contributes **at most one** preimage of $v$ (the unique solution of $A^i z=v$ lying in $C_i$). Outside $Q$, $f=\mathrm{id}$ contributes one preimage exactly when $v\notin Q$.

*Interior of $Q_1$:* $v$ lies in the images of $C_1$ and $C_5$ only. The two preimages lie in $C_1=\operatorname{pos}(x^1,x^2)$ and $C_5=\operatorname{pos}(x^5,x^6)$, which are disjoint sectors, so they are **distinct**. Since $v\in Q$, the identity region contributes $0$. **Total: $2$.**

*Interior of $Q_2$ (resp. $Q_3$, $Q_4$):* $v$ lies in exactly one cone image ($C_2$, $C_3$, $C_4$ resp.), giving $1$ preimage in $Q$. Also $v\notin Q$, so the identity contributes $1$ more (the point $v$ itself, which is distinct from the preimage in $Q$ since the latter lies in $Q$). **Total: $2$.**

*Positive $x$-axis, $v=(a,0)$, $a>0$:* In $Q_1$. From $C_1$: $A^1(a,0)=(a,0)$, preimage $(a,0)\in C_1$ (on edge $x^1$). From $C_5$: $A^5(a,4a)=(a,0)$, preimage $(a,4a)=a\,x^5\in C_5$ (on edge $x^5$). These are distinct; identity contributes $0$. **Total: $2$.**

*Positive $y$-axis, $v=(0,b)$, $b>0$:* From $C_1$: $A^1(b,b)=(0,b)$, preimage $(b,b)=b\,x^2\in C_1$. From $C_5$: $A^5(0,b)=(0,b)$, preimage $(0,b)\in C_5$ (on edge $x^6$). Distinct; identity $0$. **Total: $2$.**

*Negative $x$-axis, $v=(-a,0)$, $a>0$:* Lies in $\partial Q_2\cap\partial Q_3$. From $C_2$: $A^2(a,2a)=(-a,0)$, preimage $a\,x^3\in C_2$. From $C_3$: $A^3(a,2a)=(-a,0)$, preimage $a\,x^3\in C_3$ — the **same point** (the shared edge $x^3$, where $A^2$ and $A^3$ agree because both send $x^3\mapsto y^3$). So $1$ preimage in $Q$. Since $v\notin Q$, identity adds $v$ itself. **Total: $2$.**

*Negative $y$-axis, $v=(0,-b)$, $b>0$:* Similarly, $C_3$ and $C_4$ share edge $x^4$; $A^3(b,3b)=A^4(b,3b)=(0,-b)$, giving one preimage $b\,x^4$ in $Q$. Identity adds $v$. **Total: $2$.**

**Step 5 — The origin.** $f(0)=0$ from every piece, and $0\in Q$ so the identity region gives nothing extra: the origin has exactly **one** preimage (itself). This is why the statement excludes $v=0$.

**Conclusion.** Every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^2$ has exactly two preimages under $f$; in particular $f$ is two-to-one on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ and hence **not injective**, despite being coherently oriented (all pieces unimodular with $\det=+1$). This exhibits the failure of the converse of "injective PL map ⇒ coherently oriented" in dimension $2$. $\blacksquare$
